title: Faith in Black America
objective: After this level you can explain why independent Black churches and Black Muslim movements became pillars of Black American life.
summary: After a 1787 walkout, Richard Allen led the AME Church, organized in 1816, and Black churches became community hubs. The Nation of Islam, founded in 1930, later moved toward orthodox Islam.

cards.headline: In 1787, Black worshippers walked out of a Philadelphia church.
cards.body: What they built next became a pillar of Black American life. This level follows it, and a second movement that began in Detroit.

cards.headline: A church of their own
cards.body: In 1787 Black worshippers left St. George's Methodist Episcopal Church in Philadelphia over restrictions on where they could sit. Richard Allen, formerly enslaved, became their leader. In 1816 he was consecrated bishop of the newly organized African Methodist Episcopal Church, the first African American denomination organized in the United States.

cards.headline: More than Sunday
cards.body: Churches founded by free African American Christians became the hub of Black economic, social and intellectual life in many places. They opened doors for women, if slowly. Allen first told Jarena Lee that the church's rules did not call for women preachers; in 1819 he authorized her to preach, the first woman licensed by the AME Church.

cards.headline: Islam in Black America
cards.body: In 1930 Wallace D. Fard founded the Nation of Islam in Detroit. Under Elijah Muhammad, its leader from 1934, it preached racial unity, self-help and Black-owned businesses, and members often took an X in place of surnames lost in slavery. After Elijah Muhammad died in 1975, his son Warith Deen Mohammed moved followers toward orthodox Islam, and most joined the wider Muslim community.

cards.headline: Faith in Black America: the takeaways
learned: Richard Allen led the AME Church, organized in 1816
Black churches became hubs of community life
The Nation of Islam later moved toward orthodox Islam

questions.prompt: What was the first African American denomination organized in the United States?

options.label: The Nation of Islam
options.rationale: It began in 1930, and it isn't a Christian denomination.

options.label: The Seventh-day Adventist Church
options.rationale: It was organized at Battle Creek in 1863.

options.label: St. George's Methodist Episcopal Church
options.rationale: That's the church Black worshippers left in 1787.

questions.explanation: The AME Church, organized in 1816 with Richard Allen as bishop, was the first African American denomination in the US.

questions.prompt: How did Warith Deen Mohammed change the Nation of Islam after 1975?

options.label: He moved its followers toward orthodox Islam
He moved its headquarters from Detroit to Philadelphia
options.rationale: The change was in teaching, not location.

options.label: He merged it into the AME Church
options.rationale: It moved toward Islam, not Methodism.

options.label: He replaced Islam with Rastafari
options.rationale: Most members joined the wider Muslim community.

questions.explanation: After 1975 Warith Deen Mohammed moved followers toward orthodox Islam; most joined the wider Muslim community.

questions.prompt: Level 1 said every religious movement lives in a community. What did independent Black churches become for their communities?

options.label: Places that opened only on major holidays
options.rationale: They were at the center of daily life.

options.label: The hub of economic, social and intellectual life
Private clubs with no role outside worship
options.rationale: Their role reached far beyond worship.

questions.explanation: Churches founded by free African American Christians became hubs of economic, social and intellectual life.
